title: ECG Interpretation
summary: The same read every time: rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, morphology, ST and T. Every rhythm and pattern described precisely enough in words that you can name it from a strip you have never seen.

lessons.title: The read you run every single time
lessons.body:
## The paper is a ruler

An ECG is a voltage graph printed at a fixed speed, so distance on the paper is time. At the standard `25 mm/s`:

- one small box is `1 mm` wide, which is `0.04` seconds
- one large box is `5` small boxes, which is `0.20` seconds
- five large boxes is `1.00` second

Vertically, standard calibration makes `10 mm` equal `1 mV`. Check the calibration box at the left edge of the tracing before you call anything high or low voltage, because a machine set to half standard makes normal look small.

## Six steps, the same order, forever

1. **Rate**
2. **Rhythm**
3. **Axis**
4. **Intervals** (PR, QRS, QT)
5. **Morphology** (P waves, Q waves, R-wave progression, hypertrophy)
6. **ST segments and T waves**

Then a seventh that beats all six: **compare to the old ECG**. A T-wave inversion that has been there since 2019 is wallpaper. The same inversion that is new is a phone call.

> **Key:** The value of a system is that it finds the second abnormality. The obvious finding grabs your eye and stops your search, which is exactly how a hyperkalemic patient gets read as a bundle branch block.

## Three ways to get the rate

**The sequence method.** Find an R wave that lands on a heavy line, then name each following heavy line: `300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50`. Where the next R wave lands is the rate. It is fast, it is accurate enough, and it only works on a regular rhythm.

**The 1500 method.** Count the small boxes between two R waves and divide `1500` by that number. Seventeen small boxes gives `1500 / 17`, about `88`. Use it when you need precision.

**The 6-second method.** Most strips have marks every `3` seconds at the top. Count the QRS complexes in `6` seconds and multiply by `10`. This is the only honest method for an **irregular** rhythm, because with an irregular rhythm there is no single R-to-R interval to measure.

## Regular, or not

March two R-to-R intervals off on a piece of paper and walk it down the strip. Three patterns exist:

- **Regular:** every interval identical.
- **Regularly irregular:** a repeating pattern, such as grouped beats or every third beat dropped.
- **Irregularly irregular:** no pattern at all. In practice this means atrial fibrillation, multifocal atrial tachycardia, or frequent ectopy.

## The rhythm question, in eight words

"A P for every QRS and a QRS for every P." If both halves are true, at a normal rate, with a normal PR interval, the rhythm is sinus.

When a half fails, the failure names the problem. P waves with no QRS after them means a block. QRS complexes with no P in front means the beat started below the atria, in the junction or the ventricle. No P waves at all means the atria are not organized.

## Which lead to look at

The six limb leads (`I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF`) look at the heart in the frontal plane, front-on. The six chest leads (`V1` through `V6`) cut a horizontal slice.

**Lead II** is the workhorse for rhythm because it lies nearly parallel to normal atrial depolarization, giving the clearest upright P wave. **V1** is the best lead for QRS shape, which is why bundle branch blocks and wide-complex tachycardias are sorted there.

> **Trap:** Never diagnose from one lead. A flat line in lead III alone is a disconnected electrode, not asystole, and a single lead can hide ST elevation that is obvious two leads over.
keyPoints: At 25 mm/s, a small box is 0.04 s and a large box is 0.20 s; check the calibration box before calling voltage abnormal
Read in the same order every time: rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, morphology, ST and T, then compare to the old ECG
Rate methods: 300-150-100-75-60-50 for regular, 1500 divided by small boxes for precision, 6-second count times 10 for irregular
A P for every QRS and a QRS for every P defines sinus rhythm
Lead II is best for P waves and rhythm; V1 is best for QRS morphology

checks.q: R waves fall exactly 4 large boxes apart. What is the rate?
checks.why: Counting heavy lines from an R wave gives 300, 150, 100, 75. The fourth heavy line is 75. You can check it: 4 large boxes is 0.80 seconds, and 60 divided by 0.80 is 75.

checks.q: A rhythm is irregularly irregular. Which rate method is valid?
choices: The 1500 method using one R-to-R interval
Counting complexes in 6 seconds and multiplying by 10
Any of them, since they all agree
checks.why: The sequence and 1500 methods both assume one representative R-to-R interval, which does not exist in an irregular rhythm. Counting over 6 seconds averages the variation, which is why it is the only honest choice here.

checks.q: Why does comparison to a prior ECG rank alongside the formal read?
choices: It saves time so the formal read can be skipped
It separates new changes, which are actionable, from chronic findings that are not
Old ECGs are more accurate than new ones
checks.why: Many abnormalities, such as T-wave inversions, bundle branch blocks, and Q waves, are either an emergency or meaningless depending entirely on whether they are new. The old tracing is often the single most useful piece of data available.

lessons.title: P waves, the PR interval, and the AV blocks
lessons.body:
## What a normal P wave looks like

The P wave is atrial depolarization spreading from the sinus node in the high right atrium downward and leftward. Because lead II points down and to the left, a sinus P wave is **upright in II** and, because aVR looks from the opposite shoulder, **inverted in aVR**. If that pair is not true, the beat did not start in the sinus node.

A normal P is under `0.12` seconds wide and under `2.5 mm` tall.

- **Right atrial enlargement:** a tall, peaked P over `2.5 mm` in lead II, called P pulmonale. Think COPD and pulmonary hypertension.
- **Left atrial enlargement:** a wide, notched, two-humped P in lead II, called P mitrale, with a deep terminal negative deflection in `V1`.
- **Absent P waves** with a wavy baseline means atrial fibrillation; a **sawtooth** baseline means flutter.
- **Inverted P waves** in lead II sitting just before, just after, or hidden inside the QRS mean the beat came from the junction and conducted backward into the atria.

## The PR interval is the AV node's waiting room

Measure from the start of the P to the start of the QRS. Normal is `0.12` to `0.20` seconds, that is, three to five small boxes. The delay exists so the atria can finish emptying before the ventricles contract.

## First-degree block: slow, not blocked

PR longer than `0.20` seconds, but **every P still conducts**. The name is a misnomer since nothing is actually blocked. It is usually benign and needs no treatment.

## Mobitz I (Wenckebach): it warns you

The PR interval gets **progressively longer** beat after beat until one P wave arrives and no QRS follows. Then the cycle restarts with a short PR. On the strip this looks like grouped beating, and the R-to-R intervals actually get shorter before the dropped beat.

The block sits **in** the AV node, which is richly supplied with vagal nerve endings, so atropine works and progression to complete block is uncommon. Treat only if symptomatic.

## Mobitz II: it does not warn you

The PR interval is **constant** on every conducted beat, and then a QRS simply fails to appear. No lengthening, no warning.

The block sits **below** the AV node in the His-Purkinje system, which is diseased tissue, not vagal tissue. That is why Mobitz II progresses to complete heart block without notice, why atropine often fails or paradoxically worsens it, and why the answer is pacing.

> **Key:** Wenckebach lengthens and is usually benign. Mobitz II is constant and is a pacemaker conversation. Lengthening PR equals lenient.

## Third-degree block: two independent clocks

No P wave conducts at all. The atria fire at their own regular rate and the ventricles run on an escape pacemaker at their own regular rate, with **no relationship between them**. That is AV dissociation. On the strip you see regular P waves, regular QRS complexes, a P rate faster than the QRS rate, and PR intervals that are different on every beat.

The escape rhythm tells you where the block is and how stable the patient is:

| Escape | Rate | QRS | Origin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Junctional | `40-60` | Narrow | Just below the block, higher up |
| Ventricular | `20-40` | Wide | Deep in the ventricle, unreliable |

A narrow junctional escape may tolerate atropine. A wide ventricular escape will not, because atropine acts on the AV node and the rhythm is being generated below it. Transcutaneous pacing, then a transvenous wire or permanent pacemaker, is the path.

> **Trap:** A `2:1` block, where every other P conducts with a constant PR, cannot be classified as Mobitz I or II from the strip alone, because you never see two conducted beats in a row to compare. Treat it as potentially the dangerous kind.
keyPoints: A sinus P wave is upright in lead II and inverted in aVR; anything else did not start in the sinus node
Normal PR is 0.12-0.20 s; first-degree block is longer but every P still conducts
Mobitz I lengthens progressively then drops a beat, sits in the AV node, and responds to atropine
Mobitz II has a constant PR with sudden dropped beats, sits below the node, and needs pacing
Third-degree block means AV dissociation with a junctional escape at 40-60 narrow or a ventricular escape at 20-40 wide

checks.q: A strip shows PR intervals of 0.18, 0.24, 0.32 seconds, then a P wave with no QRS, then the cycle repeats. What is this?
checks.why: Progressive PR lengthening ending in a dropped QRS, then restarting, is the definition of Wenckebach. First-degree never drops a beat, Mobitz II keeps the PR constant, and third-degree has no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes at all.

checks.q: A patient has regular P waves at 88 per minute, regular wide QRS complexes at 32 per minute, and PR intervals that differ on every beat. What is the rhythm and the best treatment?
choices: Third-degree block with a ventricular escape; transcutaneous pacing
checks.why: Independent atrial and ventricular rates with no fixed PR is complete heart block. A wide escape at 32 means the pacemaker is deep in the ventricle, below the level atropine acts on, so pacing is the intervention. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves at all.

checks.q: Why is Mobitz II more dangerous than Mobitz I?
choices: It produces a slower heart rate
Its block is below the AV node in diseased conduction tissue, so it can progress to complete block without warning
It responds only to beta blockers
checks.why: The location of the block is the whole point. Mobitz I sits in the vagally-innervated AV node and is often reversible. Mobitz II sits in the His-Purkinje system, which fails abruptly and completely, so pacing is arranged before that happens.

lessons.title: QRS width, bundle branch blocks, and axis
lessons.body:
## Width tells you where the beat started

The ventricles have a high-speed wiring system, the His-Purkinje network. A beat that uses that wiring depolarizes both ventricles almost simultaneously, producing a **narrow QRS under `0.12` seconds**, three small boxes. A narrow QRS therefore proves the beat came from above the ventricles.

A QRS of `0.12` seconds or wider means the impulse crawled through muscle instead of wiring. That happens for three reasons: the beat started in the ventricle, a bundle branch is blocked, or something is poisoning conduction, such as potassium or a sodium-channel-blocking drug.

## Right bundle branch block

The right bundle is blocked, so the right ventricle depolarizes late, by muscle-to-muscle spread from the left. The late rightward forces point toward `V1`.

- QRS `0.12` seconds or wider
- **RSR' in `V1` and `V2`**, the so-called rabbit ears: a small R, an S, then a second taller R
- A **wide slurred S wave** in leads `I`, `V5`, and `V6`
- T-wave inversion in `V1` to `V3` is expected and does not mean ischemia

## Left bundle branch block

The left bundle is blocked, so the left ventricle activates late and from the wrong direction. The late leftward forces point away from `V1` and toward `V6`.

- QRS `0.12` seconds or wider
- A **broad, notched or monophasic R wave** in `I`, `V5`, and `V6`
- A deep `QS` or `rS` complex in `V1`
- ST segments and T waves point **opposite** to the main QRS deflection, which is called appropriate discordance

> **Key:** Left bundle branch block scrambles repolarization, so it hides ordinary ischemic ST changes. The rules for finding infarction underneath it are the **Sgarbossa criteria**: ST elevation of `1 mm` or more in the same direction as the QRS (concordant), ST depression of `1 mm` or more in `V1` to `V3`, or excessively discordant ST elevation. The modified version replaces the last one with an ST-to-S ratio of `-0.25` or more negative.

A new left bundle branch block with ischemic symptoms is no longer treated as an automatic catheterization lab activation, but it is a reason for urgent evaluation rather than reassurance.

## Axis in three steps

Axis is the average direction the ventricles depolarize in the frontal plane. Normal is `-30` to `+90` degrees. You need two leads.

1. Look at the net QRS in **lead I**. Up or down?
2. Look at the net QRS in **aVF**. Up or down?
3. Read the answer.

| Lead I | aVF | Axis |
|---|---|---|
| Up | Up | Normal |
| Up | Down | Left axis deviation |
| Down | Up | Right axis deviation |
| Down | Down | Extreme axis, the northwest quadrant |

The quick refinement: if lead I is up and aVF is down, check **lead II**. If lead II is still upright, the axis is between `0` and `-30` degrees, which is physiologic, not true left axis deviation.

**Left axis deviation** suggests left ventricular hypertrophy, left anterior fascicular block, or a prior inferior infarction that removed downward forces.

**Right axis deviation** suggests right ventricular hypertrophy, acute right heart strain from pulmonary embolism, chronic lung disease, left posterior fascicular block, or a lateral infarct. It is also normal in tall thin young people and in children.

**Extreme axis**, with both lead I and aVF negative, is uncommon and points to a ventricular origin, hyperkalemia, or lead misplacement.

> **Trap:** A wide QRS is not automatically a bundle branch block. In a tachycardia it is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise, and in a sick patient with a wide, ugly, poorly-formed QRS and no clear P waves, think potassium before you think anatomy.
keyPoints: QRS under 0.12 s proves a supraventricular origin; 0.12 s or wider means ventricular origin, bundle branch block, or a conduction poison
RBBB: RSR' rabbit ears in V1 with a wide slurred S in I, V5 and V6
LBBB: broad notched R in I, V5 and V6 with a deep QS in V1, and it masks ischemia
Sgarbossa criteria find infarction under a left bundle branch block: concordant ST elevation, concordant depression in V1-V3, or excessive discordance
Axis from leads I and aVF: both up normal, I up and aVF down left, I down and aVF up right, both down extreme

checks.q: A QRS is 0.14 s wide with an RSR' in V1 and a broad slurred S wave in V6. What is it?
checks.why: Late rightward forces produce the second R wave in V1 and the reciprocal wide S in the leftward leads I, V5 and V6, which is right bundle branch block. LBBB gives a broad monophasic R in V6 and a deep QS in V1, and WPW shows a short PR with a delta wave.

checks.q: Lead I is predominantly negative and aVF is predominantly positive. What is the axis?
checks.why: A negative lead I means forces point rightward and a positive aVF means they point downward, which places the axis in the right inferior quadrant: right axis deviation. Causes include right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary embolism, and chronic lung disease.

checks.q: Why does a left bundle branch block make ordinary ST-elevation criteria unusable?
choices: Abnormal depolarization forces abnormal repolarization, so discordant ST shifts are expected at baseline
checks.why: When the ventricle depolarizes abnormally it also repolarizes abnormally, producing baseline ST and T changes opposite to the QRS. Sgarbossa criteria exist precisely to distinguish that expected discordance from a real infarction.

lessons.title: Sinus, atrial, and junctional rhythms
lessons.body:
## The sinus rhythms

**Normal sinus rhythm:** upright P in II, one P per QRS, PR `0.12-0.20`, rate `60-100`.

**Sinus tachycardia:** the same picture above `100`. It is a symptom, never a diagnosis. Fever, pain, hypovolemia, bleeding, anemia, hypoxia, pulmonary embolism, thyrotoxicosis, stimulants, and alcohol withdrawal all live here. Rate rarely exceeds `220` minus age.

> **Key:** Slowing a sinus tachycardia without fixing its cause removes the compensation and drops the cardiac output. Always ask why the heart chose that rate.

**Sinus bradycardia:** the same picture below `60`. Normal in athletes and in sleep. It matters only when the patient has symptoms, meaning hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, or signs of shock.

**Sinus arrhythmia:** P-P intervals that speed up with inspiration and slow with expiration. Normal and common in the young.

**Sinus pause or arrest:** a flat gap with no P and no QRS, then the rhythm resumes. A pause over `3` seconds is significant.

## Atrial ectopy and fibrillation

**Premature atrial contraction (PAC):** an early P wave with a different shape, followed by a normal narrow QRS. Benign.

**Atrial fibrillation:** the atria quiver at `400-600` per minute, so there are no organized P waves, only a wavering baseline, and the AV node passes impulses erratically. The result is the one description that names it on sight: **irregularly irregular with no P waves**.

Management has three forks. Rate control with a beta blocker such as metoprolol `5 mg IV` or a calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem `0.25 mg/kg IV`. Rhythm control with an antiarrhythmic. Or cardioversion, which is safe without prior anticoagulation only when onset is clearly under `48` hours, otherwise the patient needs `3` weeks of anticoagulation or a transesophageal echocardiogram to exclude an atrial clot.

Stroke risk is scored with **CHA2DS2-VASc**: congestive heart failure `1`, hypertension `1`, age `75` or older `2`, diabetes `1`, prior stroke or TIA `2`, vascular disease `1`, age `65-74` `1`, female sex `1`. A score of `2` or more in men, or `3` or more in women, means anticoagulation.

**Atrial flutter:** one re-entry circuit in the right atrium firing about `300` times a minute produces a **sawtooth baseline**, best seen in `II, III, aVF`. The AV node usually conducts every second beat, giving a ventricular rate near `150`.

> **Trap:** Any regular narrow tachycardia sitting at almost exactly `150` is flutter with `2:1` conduction until you prove otherwise. The flutter waves hide inside the QRS and T waves.

**Multifocal atrial tachycardia:** an irregular rhythm above `100` with at least **three different P wave shapes** and varying PR intervals. It is a lung disease rhythm, classically severe COPD, and the treatment is the lung, not the heart.

## Supraventricular tachycardia

What people mean by SVT is usually **AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia**: a circuit that spins inside the AV node itself. The strip shows a **regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at `150` to `250`** with no visible P waves, because the retrograde P is buried in the QRS.

The treatment ladder:

1. **Vagal maneuvers.** The modified Valsalva, where the patient strains and is then laid flat with legs raised, converts roughly `43%`.
2. **Adenosine `6 mg` rapid IV push** followed by a fast saline flush, then `12 mg` if needed. Its half-life is under `10` seconds, so a slow push does nothing. Warn the patient about the brief awful chest pressure and the pause that follows.
3. **Synchronized cardioversion** at `50-100 J` if the patient is unstable.

## Junctional rhythms

When the sinus node fails or is blocked, the AV junction takes over at its intrinsic rate. The QRS stays narrow because the ventricles are still wired normally. P waves are inverted in lead II and may appear just before the QRS, just after it, or not at all.

- **Junctional escape rhythm:** `40-60`, a safety net
- **Accelerated junctional rhythm:** `60-100`
- **Junctional tachycardia:** `100-140`, often from digoxin toxicity or after cardiac surgery
keyPoints: Sinus tachycardia is a symptom with a cause; find it rather than treating the number
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; cardioversion without anticoagulation is only safe under 48 hours of onset
CHA2DS2-VASc of 2 or more in men, 3 or more in women, means anticoagulation
A regular narrow tachycardia at almost exactly 150 is atrial flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise
AVNRT is regular, narrow, 150-250 with no visible P: vagal, then adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg, then cardioversion at 50-100 J if unstable

checks.q: A rhythm strip shows an irregularly irregular ventricular response at about 130 with a wavering baseline and no identifiable P waves. What is it?
choices: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response
checks.why: No organized P waves anywhere plus irregular irregularity is atrial fibrillation. Flutter has sawtooth waves, multifocal atrial tachycardia has three or more distinct P morphologies, and sinus tachycardia has a consistent upright P in lead II.

checks.q: Adenosine 6 mg is pushed slowly over 30 seconds through a hand IV with no effect. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The dose was too low and 18 mg is needed
Adenosine has a half-life under 10 seconds, so it was metabolized before reaching the heart
Adenosine does not work on AVNRT
The rhythm must be ventricular tachycardia
checks.why: Adenosine is destroyed in seconds by red cells and endothelium, so it must be given as a rapid push at a proximal site with an immediate saline flush. A slow peripheral push is the commonest reason a correct drug appears to fail.

checks.q: A 68-year-old with COPD has an irregular rhythm at 118 with at least three distinct P wave morphologies and varying PR intervals. What is the rhythm and the treatment?
choices: Atrial fibrillation; anticoagulate and rate control
Multifocal atrial tachycardia; treat the underlying pulmonary disease
checks.why: Three or more P morphologies with an irregular rate above 100 defines multifocal atrial tachycardia, which is driven by hypoxia, hypercapnia, and beta agonists. Wandering atrial pacemaker is the same picture at a rate under 100. Beta blockade in bronchospasm is a poor choice.

lessons.title: Ventricular rhythms, arrest rhythms, and pacemakers
lessons.body:
## Premature ventricular contractions

A PVC is a beat born in ventricular muscle. It arrives early, has **no P wave in front of it**, is **wide and bizarre**, over `0.12` seconds, and is followed by a full compensatory pause because the next sinus beat lands on refractory tissue.

Patterns worth naming: **bigeminy** is every other beat, **trigeminy** is every third, a **couplet** is two in a row, and three or more in a row is by definition ventricular tachycardia. **Multifocal** PVCs have different shapes, meaning multiple irritable sites. **R-on-T** is a PVC that lands on the preceding T wave, during the vulnerable repolarization window, and can trigger ventricular fibrillation.

## Ventricular tachycardia

**Monomorphic VT:** three or more consecutive ventricular beats, rate `100-250`, wide QRS, and every complex the same shape. It comes from a re-entry circuit around scar, so prior myocardial infarction and cardiomyopathy are the usual hosts.

**Polymorphic VT** changes shape beat to beat. When it twists around the baseline like a ribbon, with the amplitude waxing and waning, it is **torsades de pointes**, and it is bound to a long QT interval from congenital syndromes, drugs, hypokalemia, or hypomagnesemia. Treatment is **magnesium sulfate `2 g IV`** over a few minutes plus electrolyte correction, with defibrillation if there is no pulse.

> **Key:** A wide-complex tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise, especially in anyone with a prior myocardial infarction. Findings that clinch VT: AV dissociation with independent P waves marching through, fusion or capture beats, a QRS wider than `0.16` seconds, and an extreme axis.

## The arrest rhythms

**Ventricular fibrillation:** chaotic irregular waves with no identifiable QRS. Coarse VF has large amplitude, fine VF has small amplitude and usually means a longer downtime. The only treatment is CPR and defibrillation.

**Idioventricular rhythm:** a wide escape at `20-40`, the last resort pacemaker. **Accelerated idioventricular rhythm** is the same wide complex at `50-100`, and it classically appears after successful reperfusion of a coronary artery. It is usually benign and self-limited, so do not suppress it.

**Asystole:** a flat or nearly flat line. Confirm in two leads and check the gain and the electrodes before you believe it.

**Pulseless electrical activity (PEA):** organized-looking electrical activity on the monitor with no palpable pulse. The rhythm is not the problem, the cause is, and the list is the **H's and T's**:

| H's | T's |
|---|---|
| Hypovolemia | Tension pneumothorax |
| Hypoxia | Tamponade, cardiac |
| Hydrogen ion, acidosis | Toxins |
| Hypo- and hyperkalemia | Thrombosis, coronary |
| Hypothermia | Thrombosis, pulmonary |

## Paced rhythms

A pacemaker leaves a **spike**, a thin vertical mark, wherever it fires. An atrial spike is followed by a P wave; a ventricular spike is followed by a wide QRS that usually looks like a left bundle branch block, because the lead sits in the right ventricle and the left ventricle is activated late.

Three malfunctions are recognizable:

- **Failure to capture:** a spike with no P or QRS after it. The stimulus fired but the muscle did not answer.
- **Failure to sense (undersensing):** spikes appearing in the wrong places because the device cannot see the patient's own beats. This risks an R-on-T spike.
- **Oversensing:** the device mistakes noise for beats and withholds pacing, producing pauses.

A magnet placed over a pacemaker switches it to an asynchronous mode, pacing at a fixed rate regardless of the patient's own rhythm. Over an implantable defibrillator, a magnet **suspends shock therapy** without changing pacing, which is what you want when a device is shocking a patient inappropriately.

> **Trap:** Modern devices use bipolar leads whose spikes can be tiny or invisible on some monitors. A wide QRS with a left bundle pattern in a patient with a chest scar deserves a hard look for pacing before it is called a bundle branch block.
keyPoints: A PVC is early, wide, and has no P wave in front; R-on-T can trigger ventricular fibrillation
Torsades is polymorphic VT twisting around the baseline with a long QT, treated with magnesium sulfate 2 g IV
Wide-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise; AV dissociation, fusion beats, and QRS over 0.16 s confirm it
PEA is a cause hunt, not a rhythm problem: run the H's and T's
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm at 50-100 after reperfusion is benign and should not be suppressed

checks.q: A wide regular tachycardia at 170 appears in a 66-year-old with a prior anterior myocardial infarction. Independent P waves can be seen marching through the complexes. What is it?
choices: Atrial flutter with a bundle branch block
checks.why: AV dissociation, meaning P waves at their own rate unrelated to the QRS complexes, is essentially diagnostic of ventricular tachycardia, and a prior infarct supplies the scar for the circuit. Accelerated idioventricular rhythm runs at 50-100, not 170.

checks.q: A patient on high-dose haloperidol and with a potassium of 2.9 develops a polymorphic wide tachycardia that twists around the baseline. What is the first drug?
checks.why: This is torsades de pointes from a drug-induced and hypokalemia-induced long QT. Magnesium 2 g IV is first line even when the magnesium level is normal. Amiodarone prolongs the QT further and would worsen it, and adenosine has no role in a ventricular rhythm.

checks.q: The monitor shows organized narrow complexes at 50 but no pulse is palpable. What is the correct framing?
choices: Pulseless electrical activity; start CPR and search the H's and T's
checks.why: Organized electrical activity without a pulse is PEA, and survival depends on identifying a reversible cause from the H's and T's such as hypovolemia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, or massive pulmonary embolism. Atropine has no role in pulseless arrest.

lessons.title: ST elevation: criteria, leads, and the artery
lessons.body:
## What the ST segment is

The ST segment runs from the **J point**, the exact corner where the QRS stops, to the beginning of the T wave. It represents the moment when the whole ventricle is depolarized and no current should be flowing, so it should sit level with the baseline drawn between beats.

When a coronary artery occludes completely, the full thickness of muscle it supplies is injured, and the injured tissue leaks current that pushes the ST segment up in the leads facing it.

Measure elevation **at the J point**, relative to the flat segment between the end of the T wave and the next P wave.

## The criteria, with the numbers

New ST elevation at the J point in **two anatomically contiguous leads**:

| Leads | Threshold |
|---|---|
| All leads except `V2-V3` | `1 mm` (`0.1 mV`) |
| `V2-V3`, men `40` and older | `2 mm` |
| `V2-V3`, men under `40` | `2.5 mm` |
| `V2-V3`, women any age | `1.5 mm` |

The `V2-V3` exception exists because healthy young men normally have some elevation there, and applying a flat `1 mm` rule would send the entire male population to the catheterization lab.

## Contiguous means neighboring territory

- `II, III, aVF` - inferior wall
- `V1, V2` - septum
- `V3, V4` - anterior wall
- `I, aVL, V5, V6` - lateral wall

## Reciprocal change is your confirmation

A lead looking at the opposite side of an injured wall records a mirror image, so ST **depression** appears there. Reciprocal depression greatly increases confidence that elevation is a true occlusion and not a mimic.

- Inferior elevation in `II, III, aVF` produces reciprocal depression in `I` and `aVL`.
- Anterior elevation produces reciprocal depression in `II, III, aVF`.

> **Key:** Elevation without reciprocal change is where mimics live. Elevation with clear reciprocal change is an occlusion until proven otherwise.

## Which artery, and why it matters

**Inferior, `II, III, aVF`:** the right coronary artery in roughly `80%` of people, the circumflex in the rest. Two specific dangers follow. The right coronary usually supplies the sinus and AV nodes, so **bradycardia and heart block** are common. And when elevation is greater in `III` than in `II`, with reciprocal depression in `I` and `aVL`, get **right-sided leads** and look at `V4R`.

> **Trap:** A right ventricular infarct depends entirely on preload. Nitroglycerin drops preload and can cause abrupt, profound hypotension. In inferior STEMI, check `V4R` and give fluid before you reach for nitrates.

**Septal and anterior, `V1` through `V4`:** the left anterior descending artery. This is the largest territory, the one that produces pump failure and cardiogenic shock.

**Lateral, `I, aVL, V5, V6`:** the left circumflex, or a diagonal branch of the LAD.

**Posterior:** no standard lead looks at the back of the heart, so it shows up backwards in `V1` to `V3` as **tall R waves with ST depression and upright T waves**. Confirm by placing posterior leads `V7`, `V8`, `V9` around the left side, where `0.5 mm` of elevation is diagnostic. Posterior infarcts usually accompany inferior or lateral ones and are easy to dismiss as anterior ischemia.

## The clock

STEMI is a plumbing emergency measured in minutes of muscle. At a hospital that performs percutaneous coronary intervention the target is **door to balloon within `90` minutes**. If the patient must be transferred, the target is `120` minutes from first medical contact. Where timely intervention is impossible, fibrinolysis is given with a target of **door to needle within `30` minutes**.
keyPoints: Measure ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads: 1 mm everywhere except V2-V3, where it is 2 mm in men 40 and older, 2.5 mm in younger men, and 1.5 mm in women
Lead groups: II/III/aVF inferior, V1-V2 septal, V3-V4 anterior, I/aVL/V5-V6 lateral
Reciprocal ST depression strongly supports true occlusion; elevation without it suggests a mimic
Inferior STEMI is usually the right coronary artery: check V4R, expect heart block, and avoid nitroglycerin if the right ventricle is involved
Posterior MI appears as tall R waves with ST depression in V1-V3 and is confirmed with V7-V9

checks.q: A 58-year-old man has 3 mm of ST elevation in II, III and aVF with 2 mm of ST depression in I and aVL. Elevation is greater in III than II. What is the next step?
choices: Obtain right-sided leads and look at V4R before giving nitrates
Call it pericarditis because of the inferior changes
Repeat the ECG in one hour
checks.why: Inferior elevation greater in III than II with reciprocal depression in I and aVL points at a proximal right coronary occlusion, which risks right ventricular infarction. A preload-dependent right ventricle can crash with nitroglycerin, so V4R comes first. Pericarditis does not produce reciprocal depression.

checks.q: A 35-year-old man has 2.2 mm of ST elevation in V2 and V3 with no reciprocal changes and no symptoms. Does he meet STEMI criteria?
choices: Yes, because 1 mm in two contiguous leads is met
No, because men under 40 require 2.5 mm in V2-V3
Yes, because V2 and V3 are contiguous
No, because STEMI criteria do not apply under age 40
checks.why: The V2-V3 thresholds are age and sex specific precisely because young men often have benign elevation there. At 2.2 mm in a man under 40 the criterion of 2.5 mm is not met, and the absence of symptoms and reciprocal change makes early repolarization far more likely.

checks.q: V1 to V3 show tall R waves, 2 mm of horizontal ST depression, and upright T waves in a patient with chest pain. What should you suspect and confirm?
choices: Anterior ischemia; start a heparin drip and observe
Posterior myocardial infarction; obtain leads V7 to V9
Right bundle branch block; no action
checks.why: The back of the heart has no facing lead, so a posterior infarct appears as a mirror image in the anterior leads: tall R waves, ST depression, upright T waves. Posterior leads V7 to V9 showing 0.5 mm of elevation confirm it and change the patient from ischemia to occlusion.

lessons.title: The mimics, and the ischemia that never elevates
lessons.body:
## Five things that elevate ST segments and are not occlusions

**Pericarditis.** Inflammation of the sac touches the whole heart, so elevation is **diffuse**, appearing in most leads rather than one territory, and it is **concave upward**, like a smile. Two supporting signs: **PR segment depression** in the limb leads with PR elevation in `aVR`, and the absence of any reciprocal depression except in `aVR` and `V1`.

**Early repolarization.** Concave elevation with a notch or slur at the J point, largest in the mid-precordial leads, in young healthy people, and unchanged on every prior tracing.

**Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain.** Very tall voltage with **discordant** changes: ST elevation in `V1` to `V3` where the QRS is deeply negative, and downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T inversion in `I, aVL, V5, V6`, where the QRS is tall.

**Left bundle branch block and ventricular pacing.** Discordant ST shifts are built in, which is why Sgarbossa criteria exist.

**Left ventricular aneurysm.** Persistent ST elevation with well-formed **Q waves** in the same leads, weeks or months after an anterior infarct, unchanged over time.

**Brugada pattern.** A coved, downsloping ST elevation in `V1` and `V2` that descends into an inverted T wave, in a structurally normal heart. It is a sodium channel disease associated with sudden death, not an infarct.

> **Key:** Mimics are diffuse, concave, chronic, or unaccompanied by reciprocal depression. Occlusions are territorial, often convex or straightened, dynamic between tracings, and usually have a mirror.

## Ischemia that never elevates

When a coronary artery is severely narrowed but not completely blocked, the inner layer of muscle starves first. That produces **ST depression** and **T-wave inversion** rather than elevation.

- **ST depression** that is **horizontal or downsloping**, at least `0.5 mm` at `80` milliseconds past the J point, is the ischemic pattern. Upsloping depression is usually rate-related and much less specific.
- **T-wave inversions** that are deep and symmetric, in a coronary distribution, are ischemic. Shallow asymmetric inversions are frequently normal.

## Three patterns that are emergencies without elevation

**Wellens' syndrome.** During a **pain-free** interval after chest pain, `V2` and `V3` show either deeply symmetric inverted T waves (type B) or biphasic T waves that go up then down (type A). R waves are preserved, there are no Q waves, and troponin is normal or barely raised. This means a critical stenosis of the **proximal left anterior descending artery** that has temporarily reopened.

> **Trap:** A Wellens patient looks well and pain-free, which tempts a stress test. Stressing a critical proximal LAD stenosis can cause the infarct you were trying to predict. These patients go to catheterization.

**De Winter T waves.** Upsloping ST depression of `1` to `3 mm` at the J point in `V1` through `V6`, each rising into a **tall, symmetric, peaked T wave**, often with slight ST elevation in `aVR`. This is an LAD occlusion equivalent and is treated as a STEMI even though the criteria are not met.

**aVR elevation with diffuse depression.** ST elevation of `1 mm` or more in `aVR` together with ST depression in six or more leads suggests **left main** or severe three-vessel disease, or global supply-demand failure. It is a very sick pattern.

## How an infarct evolves

| Time | Finding |
|---|---|
| Minutes | Hyperacute T waves: tall, broad, symmetric |
| Minutes to hours | ST elevation |
| Hours to days | Q waves appear, ST begins to settle |
| Days | T-wave inversion, ST returns to baseline |
| Permanent | Q waves remain as the scar's signature |

A pathologic Q wave is at least `0.04` seconds wide or more than one quarter the height of the following R wave. Knowing the stage tells you how old the event is, which is why an ECG with Q waves and inverted T waves but no elevation means the artery closed a while ago.
keyPoints: Pericarditis: diffuse concave elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal change except aVR and V1
LVH with strain gives elevation in V1-V3 and downsloping depression with asymmetric T inversion laterally
Wellens' syndrome is deep symmetric or biphasic T waves in V2-V3 while pain-free, meaning critical proximal LAD stenosis; catheterize, do not stress test
De Winter T waves are upsloping J-point depression into tall peaked T waves across the precordium and equal an LAD occlusion
aVR elevation with depression in six or more leads suggests left main or three-vessel disease

checks.q: A 24-year-old with sharp pain worse lying flat has 1.5 mm of concave ST elevation in I, II, aVL, aVF and V3 to V6, with PR depression in the limb leads and PR elevation in aVR. What is this?
checks.why: Elevation spanning several unrelated territories, concave morphology, PR depression, and the absence of reciprocal change make pericarditis the answer. A STEMI respects a coronary territory and produces reciprocal depression. Brugada is confined to V1 and V2 with a coved shape.

checks.q: A pain-free patient has deeply inverted symmetric T waves in V2 and V3, preserved R waves, no Q waves, and a normal troponin. What must not happen?
checks.why: This is Wellens' syndrome, meaning a critical proximal LAD stenosis that has temporarily reperfused. Exercise stress can provoke re-occlusion and a large anterior infarct. The correct path is admission and angiography.

checks.q: Which ST depression pattern is most specific for ischemia?
choices: Upsloping depression that resolves as the heart rate falls
Horizontal or downsloping depression of at least 0.5 mm measured 80 ms after the J point
checks.why: Horizontal and downsloping depression is the specific ischemic morphology. Upsloping depression is usually a rate-related artifact of tachycardia, and isolated changes in a single lead such as III or aVR are nonspecific without a matching territory.

lessons.title: Electrolytes, drugs, temperature, and the QT
lessons.body:
## Potassium is written on the ECG

Potassium sets the resting membrane potential, so it rewrites the tracing in a predictable order as the level climbs. The sequence matters more than any single number, because it tells you how close to arrest the patient is.

| Level (approximate) | Finding |
|---|---|
| `5.5-6.5 mEq/L` | Tall, **peaked, narrow-based symmetric T waves**, tented, often tallest in `V2-V4` |
| `6.5-7.5` | PR interval lengthens, P waves flatten and then disappear |
| `7.0-8.0` | QRS widens into a slurred, ugly complex with no clear boundaries |
| Above `8-9` | QRS merges with the T wave into a **sine wave**, then arrest |

> **Key:** A wide, slow, bizarre rhythm with no visible P waves in a dialysis patient is hyperkalemia until proven otherwise. Give calcium first; it does not lower potassium, it protects the myocardium while the shifting drugs work.

**Hypokalemia** does the opposite: the T wave **flattens**, the ST segment sags, and a **U wave** appears after the T, sometimes taller than the T itself. The T and U merge into a long QU interval, which is the substrate for torsades.

## Calcium and magnesium move the ST segment's length

Calcium controls the plateau phase, so it changes the **length of the ST segment** and therefore the QT.

- **Hypercalcemia:** short ST segment, **short QT**.
- **Hypocalcemia:** long ST segment, **long QT**, with a normal-looking T wave pushed out to the right.
- **Hypomagnesemia:** prolongs the QT and makes potassium impossible to replace. Suspect it in every torsades.

## Hypothermia

Below about `32` degrees Celsius the tracing shows the **Osborn wave**, also called the J wave: a positive hump riding on the junction between the QRS and the ST segment, like a camel's hump. Add bradycardia, prolonged PR, QRS and QT intervals, and shivering artifact. Below `30` degrees the myocardium becomes irritable and prone to ventricular fibrillation, which is why hypothermic patients are moved gently.

## Digoxin: effect versus toxicity

**Digoxin effect** appears at therapeutic levels and is not a problem: a downsloping, **scooped ST depression** often described as a ladle or a Salvador Dali moustache, with a shortened QT and flattened T waves, mostly in the lateral leads.

**Digoxin toxicity** is different and can produce almost any rhythm, because the drug increases automaticity while slowing AV conduction. The combination of an **atrial tachycardia with AV block** is the classic. **Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia**, where the QRS axis alternates beat to beat, is nearly specific. Junctional rhythms and bradyarrhythmias are common, and acute toxicity produces **hyperkalemia**.

## The QT interval and its correction

Measure from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave, in the lead where the T ends latest, usually `II` or `V5`. The QT shortens as the heart speeds up, so it must be corrected for rate. Bazett's formula divides the QT by the square root of the R-to-R interval in seconds.

- Normal QTc: up to about `440-450 ms` in men, `460-470 ms` in women.
- Above `500 ms`: high risk of torsades de pointes.

A crude bedside check: at normal rates, the QT should be **less than half the R-to-R interval**.

> **Trap:** QT-prolonging drugs are everywhere in a hospital, and they stack. Haloperidol, ondansetron, methadone, amiodarone, sotalol, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, antipsychotics, and tricyclics all lengthen it. Tricyclic overdose additionally **widens the QRS**, and a QRS over `100 ms` there predicts seizures and arrhythmia and is treated with sodium bicarbonate.
keyPoints: Hyperkalemia sequence: peaked T waves, then PR prolongation and loss of P waves, then QRS widening, then a sine wave
Hypokalemia flattens T waves and produces U waves, setting up torsades
Hypercalcemia shortens the QT, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia lengthen it
Osborn J waves with bradycardia mean hypothermia; below 30 C the heart is VF-prone
QTc over 500 ms is high torsades risk; digoxin effect is scooped ST depression, while toxicity causes atrial tachycardia with block and bidirectional VT

checks.q: A dialysis patient who missed two sessions has a wide, slow, sinusoidal rhythm with no visible P waves. What is the first drug?
checks.why: A sine wave pattern is late hyperkalemia minutes from arrest. Calcium raises the threshold potential and stabilizes the myocardium immediately, buying time for insulin with dextrose and albuterol to shift potassium and for dialysis to remove it. Antiarrhythmics do not address the cause.

checks.q: A patient has a QT of 480 ms at a heart rate of 60. What is the QTc and how concerning is it?
choices: About 480 ms, borderline and worth reviewing QT-prolonging drugs
The QTc cannot be calculated at a rate of 60
checks.why: At a rate of 60 the R-to-R interval is 1.0 second and its square root is 1.0, so the QTc equals the QT at 480 ms. That is above the normal ceiling and below the 500 ms high-risk line, which makes it a reason to review medications and electrolytes.

checks.q: An elderly patient on digoxin has an atrial tachycardia at 170 with 2:1 AV block and a potassium of 5.9. What does this suggest?
choices: Normal aging of the conduction system
checks.why: Increased atrial automaticity combined with AV nodal blockade is the classic toxic signature, and acute digoxin toxicity drives potassium out of cells, producing hyperkalemia. Digoxin effect is a benign scooped ST depression without arrhythmia.

lessons.title: Strain, accessory pathways, and lies the machine tells
lessons.body:
## Pulmonary embolism

There is no ECG that diagnoses a clot, but there are findings that raise suspicion, and they are worth knowing in order of frequency.

1. **Sinus tachycardia** is by far the most common finding.
2. **T-wave inversions in `V1` to `V4`**, the anterior leads, reflect acute right ventricular strain. When they appear together with inferior T inversions, suspicion rises sharply.
3. **S1Q3T3**: a deep S wave in lead `I`, a Q wave in lead `III`, and an inverted T in lead `III`. Famous, taught constantly, and present in only about `10%` of cases.
4. **New right bundle branch block**, complete or incomplete, right axis deviation, and new atrial fibrillation.

> **Trap:** A completely normal ECG does not exclude pulmonary embolism. The tracing supports the diagnosis; it never rules it out.

## Wolff-Parkinson-White

An accessory bundle connects atrium to ventricle directly, bypassing the AV node's protective delay. Because part of the ventricle starts depolarizing early, through muscle rather than wiring, you see:

- a **short PR interval**, under `0.12` seconds
- a **delta wave**, a slurred, sloped upstroke at the beginning of the QRS
- a **wide QRS**, because the early slurred portion is added to the normal one

> **Key:** The emergency is atrial fibrillation in a patient with WPW. The AV node normally limits how fast impulses reach the ventricle. If you block the AV node with adenosine, diltiazem, verapamil, a beta blocker, or digoxin, every fibrillatory impulse takes the accessory pathway instead, and the ventricle can be driven into fibrillation. The strip looks like an irregular, wide, very fast tachycardia, often above `200`. Treat with procainamide or electrical cardioversion.

## The effusion pair

**Low voltage** means QRS amplitude under `5 mm` in all limb leads or under `10 mm` in all precordial leads. Causes are anything that insulates or replaces muscle: pericardial effusion, obesity, COPD, large pleural effusions, and infiltrative disease.

**Electrical alternans** is a beat-to-beat alternation in QRS **amplitude**, tall then short then tall, because the heart is literally swinging inside a fluid-filled sac. Low voltage plus electrical alternans plus tachycardia is the ECG of a large effusion with tamponade physiology, and the next step is bedside echocardiography.

## Hypertrophy

**Left ventricular hypertrophy** is a voltage diagnosis. The most used rule is **Sokolow-Lyon**: the S wave in `V1` plus the tallest R in `V5` or `V6` totaling more than `35 mm`. An R wave in `aVL` over `11 mm` also qualifies. Add the strain pattern described earlier when it is severe.

**Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** shows hypertrophy voltage plus **deep, narrow Q waves** in the lateral and inferior leads, from the thickened septum depolarizing abnormally. The apical variant produces giant symmetric T-wave inversions across the precordium.

## When the tracing is lying

**Artifact.** A tremor, shivering, or Parkinsonian baseline creates rapid oscillations that can mimic atrial flutter or even ventricular tachycardia. The tell is that normal QRS complexes can still be marched through the noise at a regular rate, and the patient is sitting up talking to you. A flat line in one lead only is a disconnected electrode, not asystole.

> **On shift:** Treat the patient, not the monitor. Before anyone reaches for a defibrillator because of a monitor tracing, someone touches the patient and feels for a pulse.

**Lead reversal.** The commonest is left arm and right arm swapped, which produces a **negative P wave and negative QRS in lead `I`** while the chest leads stay completely normal. Lead `aVR` may look like a normal lead I should. This mimics dextrocardia, but in true dextrocardia the precordial leads also lose their normal R-wave growth, showing shrinking R waves from `V1` to `V6`. If lead I is upside down and the chest leads are normal, check the arms before you diagnose anything.
keyPoints: In PE, sinus tachycardia is most common and T inversions in V1-V4 reflect right heart strain; S1Q3T3 appears in only about 10%
WPW is a short PR under 0.12 s with a delta wave; AV nodal blockers in WPW with atrial fibrillation can cause ventricular fibrillation
Low voltage plus electrical alternans plus tachycardia means a large pericardial effusion with tamponade
Sokolow-Lyon: S in V1 plus R in V5 or V6 over 35 mm suggests left ventricular hypertrophy
A negative P and QRS in lead I with normal chest leads is arm lead reversal, not dextrocardia

checks.q: A patient with WPW develops an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 240. Which drug is contraindicated?
checks.why: Atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway is accelerated by AV nodal blockade, because blocking the node pushes every impulse into the bypass tract and can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. Procainamide slows the accessory pathway, and cardioversion is always acceptable.

checks.q: An ECG shows QRS complexes under 5 mm in all limb leads, alternating tall and short amplitude beat to beat, and a rate of 122. What should happen next?
choices: Bedside echocardiography for pericardial effusion and tamponade
Give a beta blocker for the tachycardia
Repeat the ECG with double standardization and no further action
checks.why: Low voltage with electrical alternans and tachycardia is the classic triad of a large pericardial effusion with the heart swinging in fluid. Echocardiography confirms it and assesses for tamponade. Beta blockade removes the compensatory tachycardia a tamponaded patient depends on.

checks.q: Lead I shows an inverted P wave and a negative QRS, while V1 to V6 show entirely normal R-wave progression. What is the explanation?
choices: Left and right arm lead reversal
checks.why: Swapping the arm electrodes inverts lead I but leaves the chest leads untouched, because those electrodes were not moved. In true dextrocardia the precordial leads also show reverse R-wave progression, with R waves shrinking from V1 to V6.

lessons.title: From the strip to the algorithm
lessons.body:
## Why recognition is the whole game

Every ACLS algorithm branches on two questions you answer at the bedside: **is there a pulse**, and **is the patient stable**. The rhythm narrows the choices, but those two questions choose the branch. Instability means hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure caused by the rhythm.

## Tachycardia with a pulse

A rate above `150` is usually where a tachycardia becomes the cause of trouble rather than the response to it.

**Unstable, at any width:** synchronized cardioversion. Sedate if there is time.

| Rhythm | Initial biphasic energy |
|---|---|
| Narrow and regular, such as AVNRT | `50-100 J` |
| Narrow and irregular, atrial fibrillation | `120-200 J` |
| Wide and regular, monomorphic VT with a pulse | `100 J` |
| Wide and irregular, polymorphic | Defibrillate, **unsynchronized**, at full dose |

> **Key:** Polymorphic VT is never synchronized. The machine cannot find a consistent R wave to time the shock against, so it may fail to fire at all. Irregular and wide means defibrillate.

**Stable and narrow:** vagal maneuvers first, then adenosine `6 mg` rapid IV push with an immediate flush, then `12 mg`. If it is atrial fibrillation or flutter, rate control with a beta blocker or diltiazem instead.

**Stable and wide:** treat as ventricular tachycardia. Options are an antiarrhythmic infusion, commonly amiodarone `150 mg` over `10` minutes, or procainamide or sotalol, with expert consultation. Adenosine may be considered only when the rhythm is regular and monomorphic.

## Bradycardia with a pulse

If the rate is under `50` and the patient is symptomatic **because of it**:

1. **Atropine `1 mg IV`**, repeated every `3-5` minutes to a maximum of `3 mg`.
2. If atropine fails: **transcutaneous pacing**, or **dopamine `5-20 mcg/kg/min`**, or **epinephrine `2-10 mcg/min`**.

> **Trap:** Atropine works at the AV node. In Mobitz II and in third-degree block with a wide ventricular escape, the problem is below the node, so atropine usually fails and can occasionally speed the atria while the ventricles stay slow. Go to pacing early in those rhythms.

## Cardiac arrest

The first fork is whether the rhythm is shockable.

**Shockable: ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia.**

1. High-quality CPR, minimizing interruptions.
2. **Defibrillate** at `120-200 J` biphasic, per the manufacturer, or `360 J` monophasic. Resume compressions immediately without checking a pulse.
3. **Epinephrine `1 mg IV or IO` every `3-5` minutes**.
4. **Amiodarone `300 mg`** after the third shock, with a second dose of `150 mg`, or lidocaine `1-1.5 mg/kg` then `0.5-0.75 mg/kg`.
5. Rhythm check every `2` minutes, changing compressors each time.

**Non-shockable: asystole and PEA.**

1. High-quality CPR.
2. **Epinephrine `1 mg` as early as possible**, then every `3-5` minutes.
3. Hunt the reversible cause through the H's and T's. Shocking asystole does nothing.

**The CPR numbers that matter:** compressions at `100-120` per minute, depth `2` to `2.4` inches, that is `5` to `6 cm`, full chest recoil between compressions, and a compression fraction above `60%`. For an unadvanced airway, a ratio of `30:2`. With an advanced airway, continuous compressions with a breath every `6` seconds, about `10` per minute.

## After return of circulation

Get a `12`-lead immediately, because occlusion is a frequent cause and it changes where the patient goes next. Target an oxygen saturation of `92-98%` rather than `100%`, avoid hypotension with a systolic goal above `90 mmHg`, avoid hyperventilation, and use targeted temperature management in a patient who does not follow commands.
keyPoints: Unstable tachycardia means synchronized cardioversion: 50-100 J narrow regular, 120-200 J atrial fibrillation, 100 J monomorphic VT, and unsynchronized defibrillation for polymorphic
Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg, then pacing, dopamine, or epinephrine
Atropine fails in Mobitz II and wide-escape complete block because the block is below the AV node
Shockable arrest: defibrillate 120-200 J biphasic, epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes, amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg
Compressions 100-120 per minute, 2 to 2.4 inches deep, full recoil, rhythm check every 2 minutes

checks.q: A patient with a pulse has an irregular polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia at 200 and a systolic blood pressure of 72. What is delivered?
checks.why: A synchronizer needs a consistent R wave to time against, and polymorphic VT does not provide one, so the device may never discharge. Irregular plus wide plus unstable means defibrillate unsynchronized. Adenosine has no role in a ventricular rhythm.

checks.q: A patient in third-degree block with a wide escape at 28 and a systolic pressure of 78 receives 1 mg of atropine with no change. What is next?
choices: Another 3 mg of atropine at once
Transcutaneous pacing, with dopamine or epinephrine as an alternative
checks.why: The escape focus sits below the AV node, so atropine, which acts on the node, cannot speed it. Transcutaneous pacing captures the ventricle directly, and a chronotropic infusion is the alternative. Cardioversion treats a tachycardia, not a bradycardia.

checks.q: During an arrest the monitor shows asystole confirmed in two leads. Which action is correct?
choices: Defibrillate at 200 J, then resume CPR
Continue CPR, give epinephrine 1 mg, and search the H's and T's
checks.why: Asystole is non-shockable; a defibrillator cannot reorganize a heart with no electrical activity. Survival depends on high-quality compressions, early epinephrine, and finding a reversible cause. Amiodarone is for shockable rhythms.

cards.front: At standard speed, how much time is one small box and one large box?
cards.back: Paper runs at 25 mm/s. One small box is 1 mm, which is 0.04 seconds. One large box is 5 small boxes, which is 0.20 seconds. Five large boxes equal 1 second.

cards.front: What is the standard vertical calibration, and why check it?
cards.back: 10 mm equals 1 mV. A machine set to half standard makes normal voltage look low and can turn left ventricular hypertrophy into a normal-looking tracing.

cards.front: List the six steps of a systematic ECG read, plus the seventh.
cards.back: Rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, morphology, then ST segments and T waves. The seventh is comparison with the old ECG, which decides whether a finding is new.

cards.front: Recite the sequence rate method.
cards.back: From an R wave on a heavy line, the next heavy lines are 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50. Where the next R wave falls is the rate. Only valid for a regular rhythm.

cards.front: Which rate method is the only honest one for an irregular rhythm, and how does it work?
cards.back: The 6-second method: count QRS complexes between the 3-second marks across 6 seconds and multiply by 10. Irregular rhythms have no single R-to-R interval to measure.

cards.front: State the eight-word rhythm question and what each failure means.
cards.back: A P for every QRS and a QRS for every P. P without QRS means block. QRS without P means a junctional or ventricular origin. No P at all means disorganized atria.

cards.front: Which lead is best for rhythm, and which for QRS morphology?
cards.back: Lead II for rhythm, because it lies nearly parallel to atrial depolarization and gives the clearest upright P wave. V1 for QRS shape, which is where bundle branch blocks and wide tachycardias are sorted.

cards.front: What does a sinus P wave look like, and in which two leads do you confirm it?
cards.back: Upright in lead II and inverted in aVR, because depolarization spreads down and to the left from the sinus node. Under 0.12 s wide and under 2.5 mm tall.

cards.front: Contrast the P wave of right and left atrial enlargement.
cards.back: Right: tall peaked P over 2.5 mm in lead II, called P pulmonale, seen in COPD and pulmonary hypertension. Left: wide notched two-humped P in II, called P mitrale, with a deep terminal negative deflection in V1.

cards.front: What is the normal PR interval and what does the delay accomplish?
cards.back: 0.12 to 0.20 seconds, three to five small boxes. The AV node holds the impulse so the atria finish emptying into the ventricles before ventricular contraction.

cards.front: Describe first-degree AV block and its significance.
cards.back: PR longer than 0.20 seconds, but every P still conducts to a QRS. Nothing is truly blocked, only delayed. Usually benign and requires no treatment.

cards.front: Describe Mobitz I on the strip and say where the block sits.
cards.back: PR lengthens progressively beat after beat until one P drops its QRS, then the cycle restarts. Grouped beating with R-to-R intervals shortening before the drop. The block is in the AV node, so atropine works.

cards.front: Describe Mobitz II and say why it is dangerous.
cards.back: Constant PR on conducted beats, then a QRS simply fails to appear with no warning. The block is below the AV node in diseased His-Purkinje tissue, so it progresses abruptly to complete block and needs pacing.

cards.front: How do you recognize third-degree block, and what do the two escape rhythms look like?
cards.back: Regular P waves and regular QRS complexes at different rates with no fixed PR, meaning AV dissociation. Junctional escape is 40-60 and narrow; ventricular escape is 20-40 and wide.

cards.front: Why can a 2:1 AV block not be classified from the strip?
cards.back: You never see two consecutive conducted beats, so you cannot tell whether the PR was lengthening. Treat it as potentially the dangerous infranodal type.

cards.front: What does a QRS under 0.12 seconds prove?
cards.back: That the impulse used the His-Purkinje wiring, so the beat originated above the ventricles. A QRS of 0.12 s or more means ventricular origin, bundle branch block, or a conduction poison such as potassium or a sodium channel blocker.

cards.front: Describe right bundle branch block.
cards.back: QRS 0.12 s or wider, an RSR' with rabbit ears in V1 and V2, and a wide slurred S wave in leads I, V5 and V6. T inversion in V1-V3 is expected, not ischemic.

cards.front: Describe left bundle branch block.
cards.back: QRS 0.12 s or wider, a broad notched or monophasic R wave in I, V5 and V6, a deep QS in V1, and ST and T waves pointing opposite the main QRS deflection.

cards.front: What are the Sgarbossa criteria for?
cards.back: Finding infarction underneath a left bundle branch block or ventricular pacing: concordant ST elevation of 1 mm or more, concordant ST depression of 1 mm or more in V1-V3, or excessively discordant elevation. The modified version uses an ST-to-S ratio of -0.25 or more.

cards.front: How do you determine axis in three steps?
cards.back: Look at net QRS in lead I, then in aVF. Both up is normal. I up with aVF down is left axis deviation. I down with aVF up is right axis deviation. Both down is extreme axis.

cards.front: When lead I is up and aVF is down, which lead refines the answer?
cards.back: Lead II. If lead II is still upright, the axis is between 0 and -30 degrees, which is physiologic rather than true left axis deviation.

cards.front: What causes left axis deviation and what causes right?
cards.back: Left: left ventricular hypertrophy, left anterior fascicular block, prior inferior infarct. Right: right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary embolism, chronic lung disease, left posterior fascicular block, lateral infarct, and normal tall thin young people.

cards.front: Name the normal axis range in degrees.
cards.back: Minus 30 to plus 90 degrees. Beyond minus 30 is left axis deviation, beyond plus 90 is right axis deviation, and the northwest quadrant beyond plus 180 is extreme axis.

cards.front: Why is sinus tachycardia never a diagnosis?
cards.back: It is the heart compensating for something: fever, pain, hypovolemia, bleeding, anemia, hypoxia, pulmonary embolism, thyrotoxicosis, stimulants, withdrawal. Slowing it without fixing the cause removes the compensation and drops cardiac output.

cards.front: What single description identifies atrial fibrillation?
cards.back: Irregularly irregular with no organized P waves, only a wavering baseline. The atria quiver at 400-600 per minute and the AV node passes impulses erratically.

cards.front: When is cardioversion of atrial fibrillation safe without prior anticoagulation?
cards.back: Only when onset is clearly under 48 hours. Otherwise the patient needs 3 weeks of anticoagulation or a transesophageal echocardiogram to exclude an atrial clot first.

cards.front: Give the CHA2DS2-VASc components and the treatment threshold.
cards.back: Heart failure 1, hypertension 1, age 75 or older 2, diabetes 1, prior stroke or TIA 2, vascular disease 1, age 65-74 1, female sex 1. Anticoagulate at 2 or more in men, 3 or more in women.

cards.front: What rate and appearance identify atrial flutter?
cards.back: A sawtooth baseline at about 300 atrial beats per minute, best seen in II, III and aVF, usually conducting 2:1 for a ventricular rate near 150.

cards.front: A regular narrow tachycardia sits at almost exactly 150. What should you assume?
cards.back: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction until proven otherwise. The flutter waves hide inside the QRS and T waves, and a vagal maneuver or adenosine can unmask them.

cards.front: Define multifocal atrial tachycardia and its treatment.
cards.back: An irregular rhythm above 100 with at least three distinct P wave morphologies and varying PR intervals. It is a lung disease rhythm, classically severe COPD, and the treatment is the lung.

cards.front: Describe AVNRT and the treatment ladder.
cards.back: Regular narrow tachycardia at 150-250 with no visible P waves. Vagal maneuvers first, then adenosine 6 mg rapid push with a flush, then 12 mg, then synchronized cardioversion at 50-100 J if unstable.

cards.front: Give the three junctional rhythm rates and the P wave appearance.
cards.back: Junctional escape 40-60, accelerated junctional 60-100, junctional tachycardia 100-140. The QRS stays narrow and P waves are inverted in lead II, just before or after the QRS, or hidden inside it.

cards.front: What defines a PVC on the strip?
cards.back: An early beat with no P wave in front of it, a wide bizarre QRS over 0.12 seconds, and a full compensatory pause afterward.

cards.front: Define bigeminy, couplet, multifocal, and R-on-T.
cards.back: Bigeminy is every other beat a PVC, a couplet is two in a row, multifocal PVCs have different shapes from different irritable sites, and R-on-T is a PVC landing on the preceding T wave, which can trigger ventricular fibrillation.

cards.front: Describe monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and its usual substrate.
cards.back: Three or more consecutive ventricular beats at 100-250 with a wide QRS of identical shape. It is re-entry around scar, so prior myocardial infarction and cardiomyopathy are the usual hosts.

cards.front: Describe torsades de pointes and its treatment.
cards.back: Polymorphic VT that twists around the baseline with waxing and waning amplitude, bound to a long QT from drugs, congenital syndromes, hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia. Give magnesium sulfate 2 g IV and correct electrolytes; defibrillate if pulseless.

cards.front: Which findings confirm that a wide-complex tachycardia is ventricular?
cards.back: AV dissociation with independent P waves marching through, fusion or capture beats, a QRS wider than 0.16 seconds, and an extreme axis. Absent those, still treat as VT until proven otherwise.

cards.front: Contrast idioventricular and accelerated idioventricular rhythm.
cards.back: Idioventricular is a wide escape at 20-40, the last-resort pacemaker. Accelerated idioventricular is the same wide complex at 50-100, classically after successful reperfusion, usually benign and not to be suppressed.

cards.front: What is PEA, and what list do you run?
cards.back: Organized electrical activity on the monitor with no palpable pulse. Run the H's and T's: hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion, hypo- and hyperkalemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, coronary and pulmonary thrombosis.

cards.front: Name the three pacemaker malfunctions and how each looks.
cards.back: Failure to capture: a spike with no complex after it. Failure to sense: spikes landing in the wrong places because the device cannot see native beats. Oversensing: pacing withheld because noise is mistaken for beats, producing pauses.

cards.front: What does a magnet do to a pacemaker versus an implantable defibrillator?
cards.back: Over a pacemaker it forces asynchronous pacing at a fixed rate. Over a defibrillator it suspends shock therapy without changing pacing, which stops inappropriate shocks.

cards.front: Where and against what do you measure ST elevation?
cards.back: At the J point, the corner where the QRS ends, measured against the flat baseline between the end of the T wave and the next P wave.

cards.front: State the STEMI ST-elevation thresholds.
cards.back: New elevation in two contiguous leads: 1 mm everywhere except V2-V3, where it is 2 mm in men 40 and older, 2.5 mm in men under 40, and 1.5 mm in women of any age.

cards.front: List the four contiguous lead groups and their walls.
cards.back: II, III, aVF inferior. V1, V2 septal. V3, V4 anterior. I, aVL, V5, V6 lateral.

cards.front: What is reciprocal change and why does it matter?
cards.back: A lead facing the opposite side of an injured wall records the mirror image as ST depression. Inferior elevation gives depression in I and aVL; anterior elevation gives depression in II, III, aVF. Its presence argues strongly for true occlusion over a mimic.

cards.front: Which artery supplies each STEMI territory?
cards.back: Inferior: right coronary in about 80%, circumflex in the rest. Septal and anterior: left anterior descending. Lateral: circumflex or a diagonal branch.

cards.front: Why is nitroglycerin dangerous in some inferior STEMIs?
cards.back: A right ventricular infarct is preload dependent, and nitroglycerin drops preload, causing abrupt profound hypotension. Check right-sided lead V4R first and give fluid instead.

cards.front: How does a posterior MI appear, and how is it confirmed?
cards.back: As a mirror image in V1-V3: tall R waves, ST depression, and upright T waves. Confirm with posterior leads V7-V9, where 0.5 mm of elevation is diagnostic.

cards.front: Give the reperfusion time targets for STEMI.
cards.back: Door to balloon within 90 minutes at a PCI-capable hospital, 120 minutes from first medical contact if transfer is required, and door to needle within 30 minutes when fibrinolysis is used instead.

cards.front: How does pericarditis differ from STEMI on the tracing?
cards.back: Elevation is diffuse across unrelated territories and concave upward, with PR depression in the limb leads and PR elevation in aVR, and no reciprocal depression except in aVR and V1.

cards.front: Describe the LVH strain pattern.
cards.back: Very high voltage with discordant changes: ST elevation in V1-V3 where the QRS is deeply negative, and downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T inversion in I, aVL, V5 and V6 where the QRS is tall.

cards.front: How does a left ventricular aneurysm present on ECG?
cards.back: Persistent ST elevation with well-formed Q waves in the same leads, weeks to months after an anterior infarct, and unchanged on serial tracings.

cards.front: Describe the type 1 Brugada pattern.
cards.back: A coved, downsloping ST elevation in V1 and V2 that descends into an inverted T wave, in a structurally normal heart. It is a sodium channel disease associated with sudden cardiac death.

cards.front: Which ST depression morphology is ischemic?
cards.back: Horizontal or downsloping depression of at least 0.5 mm measured 80 milliseconds past the J point. Upsloping depression is usually rate related and far less specific.

cards.front: Describe Wellens' syndrome and why a stress test is the wrong move.
cards.back: Deeply inverted symmetric or biphasic T waves in V2-V3 during a pain-free interval, with preserved R waves and no Q waves. It means critical proximal LAD stenosis, and exercise can provoke the infarct. Catheterize instead.

cards.front: Describe de Winter T waves.
cards.back: Upsloping ST depression of 1-3 mm at the J point across V1-V6, each rising into a tall symmetric peaked T wave, often with slight aVR elevation. It is an LAD occlusion equivalent treated as a STEMI.

cards.front: What does ST elevation in aVR with diffuse ST depression suggest?
cards.back: Elevation of 1 mm or more in aVR with depression in six or more leads suggests left main or severe three-vessel disease, or global supply-demand failure. It is a very sick pattern.

cards.front: Put the evolution of an infarct in order.
cards.back: Hyperacute tall broad T waves in minutes, then ST elevation, then Q waves within hours to days as ST settles, then T-wave inversion, and finally Q waves that persist permanently as the scar's signature.

cards.front: What defines a pathologic Q wave?
cards.back: At least 0.04 seconds wide, that is one small box, or deeper than one quarter the height of the following R wave.

cards.front: Give the hyperkalemia progression on the ECG.
cards.back: Peaked narrow-based T waves around 5.5-6.5, then PR prolongation and loss of P waves at 6.5-7.5, then QRS widening at 7-8, then a sine wave above 8-9, then arrest.

cards.front: What does hypokalemia do to the tracing?
cards.back: Flattens the T wave, sags the ST segment, and produces a prominent U wave after the T, sometimes taller than the T. The merged T and U create a long QU interval that sets up torsades.

cards.front: How do calcium disturbances change the QT?
cards.back: Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment and therefore the QT. Hypocalcemia lengthens the ST segment and the QT, with a normal-looking T wave pushed out to the right.

cards.front: What is an Osborn wave and what does it mean?
cards.back: A positive hump at the junction of the QRS and ST segment, also called a J wave, seen in hypothermia below about 32 C, alongside bradycardia, long intervals, and shivering artifact.

cards.front: Distinguish digoxin effect from digoxin toxicity.
cards.back: Effect is benign at therapeutic levels: scooped downsloping ST depression with a short QT. Toxicity causes arrhythmias, classically atrial tachycardia with AV block and bidirectional VT, plus hyperkalemia in acute overdose.

cards.front: How is the QTc calculated and what are the thresholds?
cards.back: Bazett divides the QT by the square root of the R-to-R interval in seconds. Normal is up to about 450 ms in men and 470 ms in women; above 500 ms carries a high risk of torsades.

cards.front: Name six drug classes that prolong the QT.
cards.back: Antipsychotics including haloperidol, ondansetron, methadone, class III antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone and sotalol, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, and tricyclic antidepressants. Their effects stack.

cards.front: What does tricyclic overdose do to the QRS and how is it treated?
cards.back: It blocks sodium channels and widens the QRS. A QRS over 100 ms predicts seizures and arrhythmia, and treatment is sodium bicarbonate.

cards.front: Give the ECG findings of pulmonary embolism in order of frequency.
cards.back: Sinus tachycardia is most common, then T-wave inversions in V1-V4 from right heart strain, then S1Q3T3 in only about 10%, plus new right bundle branch block, right axis deviation, or new atrial fibrillation.

cards.front: What are the three ECG features of WPW?
cards.back: A short PR interval under 0.12 seconds, a delta wave that slurs the beginning of the QRS upstroke, and a resulting wide QRS.

cards.front: Why are AV nodal blockers dangerous in WPW with atrial fibrillation?
cards.back: Blocking the node pushes every fibrillatory impulse down the accessory pathway, which has no rate-limiting delay, and can drive the ventricle into fibrillation. Use procainamide or electrical cardioversion.

cards.front: What ECG triad suggests a large pericardial effusion with tamponade?
cards.back: Low voltage, electrical alternans with QRS amplitude alternating beat to beat as the heart swings in fluid, and sinus tachycardia. Next step is bedside echocardiography.

cards.front: Define low voltage and list its causes.
cards.back: QRS under 5 mm in all limb leads or under 10 mm in all precordial leads. Causes include pericardial effusion, obesity, COPD, large pleural effusions, and infiltrative disease such as amyloid.

cards.front: State the Sokolow-Lyon criterion for left ventricular hypertrophy.
cards.back: The S wave in V1 plus the tallest R wave in V5 or V6 totaling more than 35 mm. An R wave in aVL greater than 11 mm also qualifies.

cards.front: How do you recognize arm lead reversal, and how does it differ from dextrocardia?
cards.back: Arm reversal inverts the P wave and QRS in lead I while the chest leads stay normal. True dextrocardia also shows reverse R-wave progression, with R waves shrinking from V1 to V6.

cards.front: Give the synchronized cardioversion energies by rhythm.
cards.back: Narrow regular such as AVNRT 50-100 J, narrow irregular atrial fibrillation 120-200 J, wide regular monomorphic VT with a pulse 100 J. Polymorphic VT is defibrillated unsynchronized at full dose.

cards.front: Why is polymorphic VT never cardioverted synchronously?
cards.back: The synchronizer needs a consistent R wave to time the shock against, and polymorphic VT does not provide one, so the device may never discharge. Irregular and wide means defibrillate unsynchronized.

cards.front: Give the symptomatic bradycardia algorithm with doses.
cards.back: Atropine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg. If that fails, transcutaneous pacing, or dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min, or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min.

cards.front: Give the shockable arrest drug sequence.
cards.back: Defibrillate 120-200 J biphasic, epinephrine 1 mg IV or IO every 3-5 minutes, and amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock with a second dose of 150 mg, or lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg then 0.5-0.75 mg/kg.

cards.front: What defines instability in a tachycardia or bradycardia?
cards.back: Hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure caused by the rhythm. Instability, not the rhythm name, chooses the algorithm branch.

cards.front: Give the CPR quality numbers.
cards.back: Compressions 100-120 per minute, depth 2 to 2.4 inches or 5 to 6 cm, full recoil between compressions, compression fraction above 60%, rhythm check every 2 minutes, and 30:2 without an advanced airway.

quiz.q: On a standard tracing, R waves are separated by 15 small boxes. What is the heart rate?
quiz.why: The 1500 method divides 1500 by the number of small boxes: 1500 divided by 15 is 100. The sequence method confirms it, since 15 small boxes is exactly 3 large boxes, which is the third heavy line: 300, 150, 100.

quiz.q: A monitor shows a flat line in lead III while leads I and II continue to show normal complexes. What is happening?
choices: A disconnected or displaced electrode affecting that lead
