quiz.why: Asystole appears in every lead simultaneously, because the heart, not the wire, has stopped. A flat line confined to one lead with normal complexes elsewhere is a lead problem. This is why asystole is confirmed in two leads and by feeling for a pulse.

quiz.q: Why is comparison with a prior ECG considered part of the read rather than an optional extra?
choices: It determines whether a finding is new, which is usually what decides management
Prior tracings are recorded at a different paper speed
It is needed to calculate the axis
quiz.why: T-wave inversions, bundle branch blocks and Q waves can be lifelong or minutes old, and the management differs completely. Nothing on the tracing itself tells you which, so the old ECG often carries more information than the new one.

quiz.q: A tracing shows P waves that are inverted in lead II and upright in aVR. What does this indicate?
choices: The beat did not originate in the sinus node, or the arm leads are reversed
quiz.why: Sinus depolarization travels down and to the left, giving an upright P in II and an inverted P in aVR. The exact reversal of that pattern means either an ectopic or junctional origin with retrograde atrial conduction, or a lead placement error, and both are worth checking.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old is asymptomatic with a heart rate of 62 and a PR interval of 0.26 seconds, with every P conducting. What is the management?
choices: No treatment; this is first-degree AV block
quiz.why: First-degree block delays every impulse but blocks none, and in an asymptomatic patient with a normal rate it requires nothing beyond noting medications that slow AV conduction. Pacing and atropine treat symptomatic bradycardia, which this is not.

quiz.q: A strip shows groups of three conducted beats followed by a pause. Within each group the PR intervals measure 0.16, 0.26 and 0.36 seconds. What is the rhythm and where is the lesion?
choices: Mobitz II, below the AV node
Mobitz I, within the AV node
Third-degree block, at the bundle of His
quiz.why: Progressive PR prolongation ending in a dropped beat with grouped beating is Wenckebach, and the lesion sits in the vagally-innervated AV node, which is why it responds to atropine and rarely progresses. Mobitz II keeps the PR constant before dropping a beat.

quiz.q: A syncopal patient has a constant PR interval of 0.18 seconds with intermittent sudden loss of a QRS, and a QRS width of 0.13 seconds. What is the appropriate disposition?
choices: Observation only, since the PR is normal
Admission with pacing pads applied and pacemaker evaluation
quiz.why: A constant PR with sudden dropped beats is Mobitz II, and a widened QRS indicates infranodal disease. It progresses to complete heart block without warning and causes syncope, so pacing capability and pacemaker evaluation are required. Beta blockade would worsen conduction.

quiz.q: A QRS measures 0.13 seconds with a broad notched R wave in V6 and a deep QS complex in V1. A new ST elevation of 1 mm appears in V6, in the same direction as the QRS. What does that elevation mean?
choices: It is expected discordance and can be ignored
It is concordant elevation, a positive Sgarbossa criterion suggesting infarction
It indicates right bundle branch block
It is an artifact of lead placement
quiz.why: In left bundle branch block the ST segment normally points opposite the QRS, so elevation in a lead with a tall positive QRS is concordant and abnormal. Concordant ST elevation of 1 mm or more is the most weighted Sgarbossa criterion.

quiz.q: Lead I is positive and aVF is negative, but lead II remains upright. How is the axis described?
choices: Physiologic left axis, between 0 and minus 30 degrees
Pathologic left axis deviation requiring workup
quiz.why: The two-lead method flags anything with a positive I and negative aVF as leftward, but an upright lead II places the axis between 0 and minus 30 degrees, which is within normal limits. True left axis deviation makes lead II negative as well.

quiz.q: A hypotensive dialysis patient has a QRS of 0.18 seconds with no identifiable P waves and a rate of 44. What is the most likely cause of the wide QRS?
quiz.why: Loss of P waves with progressive QRS widening in a dialysis patient is the hyperkalemia sequence, and it is a metabolic emergency treated with calcium first. Bundle branch block does not abolish P waves, and ventricular tachycardia is fast, not 44.

quiz.q: A 62-year-old has an irregularly irregular rhythm at 142 with no P waves, hypertension, diabetes, and a prior TIA. What is his CHA2DS2-VASc score and what follows?
quiz.why: Hypertension 1, diabetes 1, and prior TIA 2 gives 4. He is under 65 and male, so no age or sex points apply. A score of 2 or more in a man means anticoagulation, and 4 makes that clear rather than optional.

quiz.q: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia sits at 148 with no visible P waves. A vagal maneuver briefly slows AV conduction and reveals a sawtooth baseline in II, III and aVF. What is the rhythm?
quiz.why: A rate near 150 with sawtooth atrial activity unmasked by AV slowing is flutter conducting 2:1 from an atrial rate near 300. AVNRT has no atrial sawtooth, sinus tachycardia shows discrete upright P waves in II, and multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular.

quiz.q: A stable patient has a regular narrow tachycardia at 186. Vagal maneuvers fail. What is the next intervention?
choices: Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push with an immediate saline flush
quiz.why: A stable regular narrow tachycardia is treated pharmacologically first, and adenosine interrupts the AV nodal re-entry circuit. It must be pushed rapidly and flushed because its half-life is under 10 seconds. Cardioversion is reserved for instability.

quiz.q: Which description best matches multifocal atrial tachycardia?
choices: Regular, narrow, 150-250, no visible P waves
Irregular, above 100, with three or more distinct P wave morphologies
Irregular with no P waves and a wavering baseline
Regular with sawtooth atrial activity at 300
quiz.why: Multiple atrial foci each produce their own P wave shape and their own PR interval, so three or more morphologies with an irregular rate above 100 is the definition. No P waves at all is atrial fibrillation, and sawtooth is flutter.

quiz.q: A monitored patient has frequent PVCs, one of which lands directly on the preceding T wave. What is the risk?
choices: It will cause a pause requiring pacing
quiz.why: The T wave marks the vulnerable period when the ventricle is partly repolarized. A depolarization arriving then can fragment into fibrillation. This is also why cardioversion is synchronized to the R wave, so a shock never lands on a T wave.

quiz.q: Ninety seconds after a coronary artery is opened in the catheterization lab, the monitor shows a wide regular rhythm at 78 with no P waves and a stable blood pressure. What is it?
choices: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm; observe without suppressing it
quiz.why: A wide rhythm at 50-100 appearing right after reperfusion is accelerated idioventricular rhythm, a benign and usually self-limited marker of a successfully opened artery. Suppressing it can remove the only working pacemaker. VT runs faster than 100.

quiz.q: A paced patient shows pacing spikes followed by nothing at all in several places on the strip. What is the malfunction?
quiz.why: A spike represents the device firing. When no P wave or QRS follows, the stimulus failed to depolarize the muscle, which is failure to capture. Failure to sense produces spikes in inappropriate places that may still capture, and oversensing withholds pacing entirely.

quiz.q: A trauma patient in arrest has organized complexes at 96 on the monitor with no pulse, distended neck veins, and absent breath sounds on the right. Which of the H's and T's is most likely?
quiz.why: PEA with unilateral absent breath sounds and distended neck veins in trauma is tension pneumothorax, which obstructs venous return. It is fixed with immediate decompression, not with drugs, which is exactly why PEA is treated as a cause hunt.

quiz.q: Which combination of leads must both show elevation for a diagnosis of inferior STEMI?
choices: Two of II, III and aVF
quiz.why: The inferior wall is viewed by II, III and aVF, and STEMI criteria require two contiguous leads within one territory. V1 and V2 are septal, V3 and V4 anterior, and I and aVL lateral, which is where reciprocal depression appears in an inferior infarct.

quiz.q: A woman of 52 has 1.7 mm of new ST elevation in V2 and V3 with reciprocal depression in II, III and aVF and ongoing chest pain. Does she meet STEMI criteria?
choices: No, because women require 2 mm in V2-V3
Yes, because the threshold for women in V2-V3 is 1.5 mm
No, because reciprocal change excludes STEMI
Yes, but only if troponin is positive
quiz.why: The V2-V3 threshold for women of any age is 1.5 mm, which 1.7 mm exceeds, and reciprocal depression supports rather than excludes occlusion. STEMI activation is an ECG and clinical decision that must not wait for troponin.

quiz.q: Inferior ST elevation is greater in lead III than in lead II, with marked reciprocal depression in aVL. The patient's blood pressure is 104/62. What should be done before nitroglycerin?
choices: Obtain right-sided leads to look for right ventricular involvement
Obtain posterior leads V7 to V9
quiz.why: That pattern suggests proximal right coronary occlusion with possible right ventricular infarction, which is preload dependent. Nitroglycerin can cause abrupt profound hypotension, so V4R is checked and fluid given first. Beta blockade is also poorly tolerated in right ventricular infarct.

quiz.q: Which artery is most often responsible for ST elevation in V1 through V4?
quiz.why: V1 to V4 view the septum and anterior wall, both supplied by the left anterior descending artery. The right coronary supplies the inferior wall in most people, and the circumflex supplies the lateral wall.

quiz.q: A STEMI patient arrives at a hospital without a catheterization lab, and the nearest PCI center is 3 hours away by ground. What is the correct reperfusion strategy?
choices: Transfer for PCI regardless of time
Fibrinolysis with a door-to-needle target of 30 minutes
quiz.why: PCI is preferred when it can be achieved within 120 minutes of first medical contact. When transfer cannot meet that window, fibrinolysis is given with a door-to-needle target of 30 minutes, then transfer. Waiting on troponin wastes myocardium.

quiz.q: Which feature most reliably separates acute pericarditis from an anterior STEMI?
choices: Diffuse concave elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal change
quiz.why: Pericarditis inflames the whole sac, producing elevation across unrelated territories with a concave shape, PR depression, and no reciprocal depression except in aVR and V1. Both conditions cause pain and can raise troponin, and elevation height distinguishes nothing.

quiz.q: A patient with chest pain has upsloping ST depression of 2 mm at the J point in V2 through V6, each leading into a tall symmetric peaked T wave, with 1 mm of elevation in aVR. What does this represent?
choices: De Winter T waves, equivalent to proximal LAD occlusion
quiz.why: De Winter T waves are a recognized STEMI equivalent from proximal LAD occlusion and are taken straight to the catheterization lab despite the absence of classic elevation. Hyperkalemic T waves are narrow-based and are not preceded by J-point depression across the precordium.

quiz.q: A pain-free patient with a recent episode of chest pain has biphasic T waves in V2 and V3 that rise then descend, with preserved R waves and a troponin at the upper limit of normal. What is the disposition?
choices: Reassurance, since the patient is pain free
Repeat the ECG in one week
quiz.why: This is type A Wellens' syndrome, which indicates a critical proximal LAD stenosis that has temporarily reperfused. Stress testing can provoke a large anterior infarct, so these patients are admitted and catheterized.

quiz.q: ST elevation of 1.5 mm in aVR accompanies ST depression in seven other leads in a hypotensive patient. What does this pattern suggest?
choices: Left main or severe three-vessel disease
quiz.why: Diffuse subendocardial ischemia produces widespread depression with reciprocal elevation in aVR, the one lead pointing in the opposite direction. It suggests left main or three-vessel disease or global supply-demand failure, and these patients are critically ill.

quiz.q: An ECG shows ST elevation with well-formed Q waves in V1 to V4 that is identical to a tracing from eight months ago, in an asymptomatic patient with a prior anterior MI. What is it?
quiz.why: Persistent ST elevation with established Q waves that is unchanged over months after an anterior infarct is an aneurysm, not a new event. The comparison tracing is what makes the diagnosis, which is why the old ECG is part of the read.

quiz.q: Which ECG change appears first as potassium rises?
quiz.why: The sequence is fixed: tented T waves around 5.5-6.5, then PR prolongation with loss of P waves, then QRS widening, then a sine wave before arrest. Recognizing the first step buys time the later steps do not allow.

quiz.q: A patient has flattened T waves, sagging ST segments, and prominent U waves after each T. Which electrolyte problem is this, and what is the main risk?
quiz.why: U waves with flattened T waves are the hypokalemia signature, and the merged long QU interval creates the substrate for torsades de pointes. Hyperkalemia peaks T waves instead, and calcium changes the QT length without producing U waves.

quiz.q: A hiker found in the snow has a core temperature of 29 C, a heart rate of 38, and a positive hump at the junction of the QRS and ST segment in multiple leads. What is the hump and what is the main precaution?
choices: A delta wave; avoid AV nodal blockers
An Osborn J wave; handle the patient gently because the myocardium is VF-prone
A pathologic Q wave; activate the catheterization lab
quiz.why: The Osborn or J wave is characteristic of hypothermia below about 32 C. Below 30 C the myocardium becomes irritable, and rough handling or jostling can precipitate ventricular fibrillation, so movement is minimized during rewarming.

quiz.q: A patient on amiodarone, ondansetron and a fluoroquinolone has a QTc of 520 ms. What is the concern and the action?
choices: No concern, since each drug alone is safe
High torsades risk; review and remove QT-prolonging drugs and correct potassium and magnesium
The QTc cannot exceed 500 ms, so the machine is wrong
quiz.why: QT-prolonging effects are additive, and a QTc above 500 ms carries a high risk of torsades de pointes. The intervention is to stop the offending drugs where possible and normalize potassium and magnesium, which shorten the QT and raise the fibrillation threshold.

quiz.q: A patient with sudden pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia has sinus tachycardia at 118 with new T-wave inversions in V1 through V4 and a new incomplete right bundle branch block. What does the ECG support?
choices: Acute right heart strain, consistent with pulmonary embolism
quiz.why: Anterior T-wave inversions with a new right bundle branch block and sinus tachycardia reflect acute right ventricular strain and support pulmonary embolism. They do not confirm it, and a normal ECG would not exclude it either, so imaging decides.

quiz.q: A patient with a known delta wave and a short PR presents with an irregular wide tachycardia at 250. Which agent is the safest choice?
quiz.why: Atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway is accelerated by any AV nodal blocker, which can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. Procainamide slows conduction in the accessory pathway itself, and electrical cardioversion is always acceptable.

quiz.q: Which ECG picture belongs to a large pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology?
choices: Tall voltage with deep lateral T inversions
Low voltage with electrical alternans and sinus tachycardia
Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Peaked T waves with a widened QRS
quiz.why: Fluid insulates the heart, lowering voltage, and the heart swinging within it alternates QRS amplitude beat to beat, while tachycardia maintains output. Diffuse elevation with PR depression is pericarditis without significant effusion, and peaked T waves are hyperkalemia.

quiz.q: A patient with a pulse has a regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia at 180, a blood pressure of 76/44, and cool mottled skin. What is the correct treatment?
quiz.why: Hypotension with signs of shock caused by the rhythm makes this unstable, so electricity replaces drugs. Monomorphic VT with a pulse is synchronized at 100 J. Unsynchronized shocks are for pulseless or polymorphic rhythms, and amiodarone is for stable patients.

quiz.q: During a cardiac arrest the rhythm check shows coarse ventricular fibrillation after two minutes of CPR and one prior shock. What is the sequence?
choices: Check a pulse, then shock, then check a pulse again
Shock immediately, resume compressions without a pulse check, and give epinephrine 1 mg
quiz.why: Ventricular fibrillation is shockable, and the shock is followed immediately by compressions rather than a pulse check, because a heart that has just been defibrillated needs perfusion. Epinephrine 1 mg is given every 3-5 minutes, and amiodarone comes after the third shock. Pacing does not treat fibrillation.

scenarios.title: Six strips: the slow side
scenarios.intro:
You are reading monitor strips on one patient over `40` minutes. Each strip is described in words and measurements. For each one, name the rhythm, then choose the first action.

The patient is a `74`-year-old man who came in feeling faint. He is awake, pale, and diaphoretic throughout unless told otherwise.

steps.prompt:
**Strip 1.** Regular. R-to-R interval `8` large boxes. Upright P wave before every QRS in lead II, one P per QRS. PR interval `0.16` seconds. QRS `0.08` seconds.

He is lightheaded and clammy.

choices.text: Sinus bradycardia with symptoms: atropine `1 mg IV`, repeatable every `3-5` minutes to `3 mg`
choices.feedback: Correct. Eight large boxes is 60 divided by 1.6 seconds, about 38. A P for every QRS with a normal PR and a narrow QRS makes it sinus, and hypotension with pallor makes it symptomatic, which is what earns atropine.

choices.text: Junctional escape rhythm: prepare for pacing
choices.feedback: A junctional escape has no upright P wave in front of the QRS, or has an inverted one. This strip has a normal sinus P with a normal PR, so the sinus node is in charge, just slowly.

choices.text: Normal for his age: no action needed
choices.feedback: A rate of 38 with a systolic of 84 and a clammy patient is symptomatic by definition. Age never makes hypoperfusion normal.

steps.prompt: **Strip 2.** After atropine the atrial rate rises to `86`. Now the PR interval measures `0.18` seconds and is **identical on every conducted beat**, but roughly every third P wave has no QRS after it at all. QRS width `0.13` seconds.

choices.text: Mobitz II: place pacing pads now and arrange for transvenous or permanent pacing
choices.feedback: Right. A constant PR with abruptly dropped beats and a widened QRS means the block is below the AV node in the His-Purkinje system. Atropine speeds the atria without helping conduction, so more of it can actually worsen the ratio.

choices.text: Mobitz I: observe, this is benign
choices.feedback: Wenckebach requires progressive PR lengthening before the drop. The PR here is fixed at 0.18 on every conducted beat, which is the defining feature of the dangerous variety.

choices.text: Third-degree block: start pacing immediately
choices.feedback: Close, and the preparation is right, but complete block means no P conducts at all and the PR varies on every beat. Here two out of three P waves still conduct with a fixed PR, so this is Mobitz II.

steps.prompt: **Strip 3.** P waves march out regularly at `88` per minute. QRS complexes march out regularly at `30` per minute and are `0.15` seconds wide. The PR interval is different on every beat, and some P waves sit inside QRS complexes and T waves.

choices.text: Give another `1 mg` of atropine and reassess in five minutes
choices.feedback: Atropine acts on the AV node, and this escape is being generated below it. Waiting five minutes at a pressure of 70 systolic costs brain and myocardium.

choices.text: Third-degree AV block with a ventricular escape: start transcutaneous pacing, with dopamine or epinephrine as an alternative
choices.feedback: Correct. Two independent regular rates with no fixed relationship is AV dissociation, and a wide escape at 30 places the pacemaker deep in the ventricle. Pacing captures the ventricle directly, which is the only reliable option.

choices.text: Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response: rate is fine, observe
choices.feedback: Atrial fibrillation has no organized P waves at all. Regular marching P waves at 88 rule it out immediately.

steps.prompt: **Strip 4.** Transcutaneous pacing is running at a set rate of `70`. Thin vertical spikes appear exactly `70` times a minute. Only about half of them are followed by a wide QRS. The patient's femoral pulse matches the complexes, not the spikes.

choices.text: Failure to capture: increase the output in milliamps until every spike produces a complex and a pulse
choices.feedback: Exactly. A spike with nothing after it means the stimulus fired but the muscle did not answer. Increase output until there is electrical capture with a matching mechanical pulse, then set the output slightly above that threshold.

choices.text: Failure to sense: reduce the sensitivity setting
choices.feedback: Failure to sense means spikes appear in the wrong places because the device cannot see the patient's own beats. Here the spikes are perfectly regular at the set rate; the problem is what happens after them.

choices.text: The pacemaker is working correctly since spikes are visible at the set rate
choices.feedback: Spikes prove the device is firing, not that the heart is beating. Capture is judged by a complex after every spike and, above all, by a palpable pulse at the paced rate.

steps.prompt: **Strip 5.** Pacing is stopped after a permanent device decision is deferred. The rhythm is now **irregularly irregular** with no identifiable P waves and a wavering baseline. Ventricular rate about `168`. He is grey, with crushing chest pressure.

choices.text: Diltiazem `0.25 mg/kg IV` for rate control
choices.feedback: Rate control is right for a stable patient, but this one is hypotensive with ischemic chest pain caused by the rate. A calcium channel blocker will drop the pressure further.

choices.text: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, unstable: synchronized cardioversion at `120-200 J` biphasic
choices.feedback: Correct. Irregularly irregular with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, and hypotension with ischemic chest pain caused by the rhythm defines instability. Electricity replaces drugs the moment instability appears.

choices.text: Adenosine `6 mg` rapid push
choices.feedback: Adenosine interrupts AV nodal re-entry circuits. Atrial fibrillation is not a re-entry circuit through the node, so at best it produces a brief revealing pause and does nothing therapeutic.

steps.prompt: **Strip 6.** Immediately after the shock the tracing shows chaotic, coarse, irregular undulations with no identifiable QRS complexes anywhere. No pulse is palpable.

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion at `200 J`
choices.feedback: There is no R wave for the synchronizer to time against, so the machine may never discharge. In a pulseless chaotic rhythm the shock must be unsynchronized.

choices.text: Ventricular fibrillation: immediate unsynchronized defibrillation at `120-200 J` biphasic with high-quality CPR, then epinephrine `1 mg` every `3-5` minutes
choices.feedback: Correct. Coarse chaotic activity with no QRS and no pulse is ventricular fibrillation, and defibrillation is the only treatment that reorganizes it. Compressions resume immediately after the shock without a pulse check.

choices.text: Check a carotid pulse for a full 60 seconds before acting
choices.feedback: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds. A prolonged check delays both compressions and the shock, and in ventricular fibrillation survival falls roughly 7 to 10 percent for every minute without defibrillation.

scenarios.debrief:
## The pattern to remember

Every strip in this case was named by two measurements and one relationship.

- **Rate** from the R-to-R interval.
- **Width** of the QRS, which says whether the beat came from above or below the ventricles.
- **The relationship between P and QRS**, which names every block.

The escalation followed conduction failing from the top down: the sinus node slowed, then the His-Purkinje system dropped beats, then it dissociated entirely, then an external pacemaker took over and had to be checked for capture, and finally the sick myocardium produced its own chaos.

> **Key:** Atropine treats the AV node. Once the block or the escape is below the node, atropine is a delay, and pacing is the treatment.

scenarios.title: Six strips: the fast side
scenarios.intro:
Six more strips, six different patients, all described in words and measurements. Name the rhythm or pattern, then choose the first action.

Nothing here requires an image. Every finding is given to you as a number, a shape, or a relationship.

steps.prompt: **Strip 1.** A `29`-year-old woman with palpitations. The rhythm is perfectly regular. QRS width `0.08` seconds. No P waves are visible anywhere. R-to-R interval is `8` small boxes.

choices.text: Regular narrow tachycardia, likely AVNRT, and she is stable: vagal maneuvers first, then adenosine `6 mg` rapid push with an immediate flush
choices.feedback: Correct. 1500 divided by 8 is about 188. Regular, narrow, fast, and no visible P because the retrograde P is buried in the QRS. A stable patient gets the modified Valsalva first, which converts roughly 43 percent.

choices.text: Sinus tachycardia: look for a cause and treat that
choices.feedback: Sinus tachycardia has a visible upright P wave in lead II and rarely reaches 188 in a 29-year-old at rest. Absent P waves at this rate with an abrupt onset points at a re-entry circuit.

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion at `100 J` now
choices.feedback: Electricity is correct only for instability. This patient has a normal blood pressure and normal mentation, so drugs and vagal maneuvers come first and sedation is avoided.

steps.prompt: **Strip 2.** Different patient. Regular rhythm, QRS `0.09` seconds, ventricular rate exactly `150`. During a vagal maneuver the ventricular rate transiently halves and the baseline in `II, III` and `aVF` shows a continuous sawtooth pattern at about `300` per minute.

choices.text: Atrial flutter with `2:1` conduction
choices.feedback: Correct. An atrial rate near 300 with the AV node passing every second impulse gives a ventricular rate near 150, and the sawtooth hides inside the QRS and T waves until the node is slowed.

choices.text: Sinus tachycardia at 150
choices.feedback: Sinus tachycardia produces one discrete upright P per QRS, not a continuous sawtooth at twice the ventricular rate. A regular narrow tachycardia sitting at exactly 150 should always prompt a hunt for flutter waves.

choices.text: Atrial fibrillation
choices.feedback: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with a chaotic baseline. This rhythm is regular with an organized repeating atrial waveform, which is the difference between one re-entry circuit and hundreds of wavelets.

steps.prompt: **Strip 3.** A patient on haloperidol and ondansetron with a potassium of `3.0`. The prior ECG showed a QTc of `540 ms`. The monitor now shows a **wide, irregular tachycardia whose peaks twist from upright to inverted and back**, with the amplitude waxing and waning around the baseline. A weak pulse is present.

choices.text: Amiodarone `300 mg IV`
choices.feedback: Harmful here. Amiodarone prolongs the QT, which is the exact substrate driving this rhythm, so it can make torsades worse.

choices.text: Torsades de pointes: magnesium sulfate `2 g IV`, correct potassium, and stop the offending drugs
choices.feedback: Correct. A twisting polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a documented long QT is torsades, and magnesium is first line even when the magnesium level is normal. Repleting potassium raises the fibrillation threshold.

choices.text: Adenosine `6 mg` rapid push
choices.feedback: Adenosine works on AV nodal re-entry. This rhythm originates in the ventricle, below the node, so adenosine has no target.

steps.prompt: **Strip 4.** A dialysis patient who missed two sessions. Rate `46`, regular. **No P waves are visible.** QRS width `0.19` seconds, and the complexes are slurred so that it is hard to say where the QRS ends and the T wave begins. An earlier strip from triage showed tall, narrow-based, peaked T waves.

choices.text: Hyperkalemia: calcium gluconate `1 g IV` first, then insulin with dextrose and albuterol, then dialysis
choices.feedback: Correct. Peaked T waves progressing to loss of P waves and a widening slurred QRS is the hyperkalemia sequence, one step from a sine wave. Calcium does not lower potassium; it stabilizes the myocardium while the shifting drugs work.

choices.text: Idioventricular rhythm: begin transcutaneous pacing
choices.feedback: The strip does look ventricular, but the story and the earlier peaked T waves name the cause. Pacing a hyperkalemic myocardium often fails to capture, and the metabolic problem remains.

choices.text: Left bundle branch block with sinus bradycardia: observe
choices.feedback: A bundle branch block does not abolish P waves. Their disappearance alongside QRS widening is the specific hyperkalemia progression, and observing it leads to a sine wave and arrest.

steps.prompt: **Strip 5.** Before treatment is given, the same patient becomes unresponsive. The monitor shows organized, wide complexes at `72` per minute that look unchanged from the previous strip. No pulse is palpable at the carotid after a `10`-second check.

choices.text: Defibrillate at `200 J` immediately
choices.feedback: There is organized electrical activity, not fibrillation. A shock does nothing to a heart whose electrical system is working and whose muscle is not responding.

choices.text: Pulseless electrical activity: high-quality CPR, epinephrine `1 mg`, and treat the H that caused it, which here is hyperkalemia, with calcium and shifting agents
choices.feedback: Correct. PEA is a cause hunt. The rhythm on the screen is not the problem, and in this patient the reversible H is sitting in plain view from the earlier strips.

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion at `100 J`
choices.feedback: Cardioversion treats an unstable tachycardia with a pulse. In pulseless arrest with organized activity, the answer is compressions, epinephrine, and the reversible cause.

steps.prompt: **Strip 6.** Circulation returns. The post-arrest `12`-lead shows `3 mm` of ST elevation in `II, III` and `aVF`, with elevation greater in `III` than in `II`, and `2 mm` of ST depression in `I` and `aVL`. Blood pressure is `98/58`.

choices.text: Give sublingual nitroglycerin for the ST elevation, then reassess
choices.feedback: Dangerous. This pattern suggests proximal right coronary occlusion with possible right ventricular infarction, which is preload dependent. Nitroglycerin can drop the pressure catastrophically.

choices.text: Inferior STEMI: activate the catheterization lab, obtain right-sided leads to check `V4R`, and give fluid rather than nitrates if the right ventricle is involved
choices.feedback: Correct. Territorial elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL is an inferior occlusion, and elevation greater in III than II points proximal in the right coronary artery. A post-arrest 12-lead is mandatory for exactly this reason.

choices.text: Call it pericarditis, since ST elevation after CPR is expected
choices.feedback: Pericarditis produces diffuse concave elevation across unrelated territories with PR depression and no reciprocal change. Elevation confined to one territory with a mirror image in another is an occlusion.

scenarios.debrief:
## The pattern to remember

Every fast rhythm is sorted by three questions, asked in this order:

1. **Is there a pulse?** No pulse with chaos means defibrillate. No pulse with organized complexes means PEA and a cause hunt.
2. **Is the patient stable?** Instability, meaning hypotension, altered mentation, shock, ischemic pain, or acute heart failure, moves you from drugs to electricity immediately.
3. **Narrow or wide, regular or irregular?** Those two answers pick the drug and the energy.

Two strips in this case were not primarily rhythm problems at all. The hyperkalemic wide bradycardia and the post-arrest inferior STEMI were metabolic and plumbing emergencies that happened to be visible on the monitor.

> **Trap:** The prettiest rhythm label is worthless if you skipped the pulse check. Touch the patient before you name the strip.
